nature-001.summary: Flowing north through northeast Africa into the Mediterranean, the lifeline that nurtured ancient Egyptian civilization and is counted as the world's longest river.
facts: Until the Aswan High Dam was built, its annual floods enriched the fields of Egypt.
Its two main branches, the White Nile and the Blue Nile, meet at Khartoum in Sudan.

nature-002.summary: Rising in the Andes and crossing northern South America to the Atlantic, the river that waters the world's largest rainforest and carries more water than any other.
facts: It carries more water than the next seven largest rivers combined.
Not a single bridge crosses its main channel.

nature-003.summary: Crossing the heart of China from the Tibetan Plateau to the sea off Shanghai, Asia's longest river, whose basin is home to nearly a third of China's people.
facts: In China, it is called the Chang Jiang, meaning “Long River.”
The Three Gorges Dam across it has the largest generating capacity of any dam in the world.

nature-004.summary: Watering the broad plains of northern India on its way to the Bay of Bengal, Hinduism's most sacred river and a lifeline for hundreds of millions.
facts: It rises at the Gangotri Glacier in the Himalayas and passes through Bangladesh before reaching the sea.
The tradition of cremation on its banks at Varanasi continues to this day.

nature-005.summary: Flowing north to south through the heart of the United States to the Gulf of Mexico, the trunk of the nation's largest drainage basin, gathering water from 32 states, and a great inland shipping route.
facts: Its name means “big river” in a Native American language.
Mark Twain's “Adventures of Huckleberry Finn” is set along its waters.

nature-006.summary: Crossing Central and Southeastern Europe from southwestern Germany to the Black Sea, once a frontier of the Roman Empire and today an international waterway linking ten countries.
facts: Four capitals lie on its banks: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.
Strauss's waltz “The Beautiful Blue Danube” sings its praises.

nature-008.summary: Rising between the plains of the Indian subcontinent and the Tibetan Plateau, the range where great rivers like the Indus and Ganges begin, their basins home to some 600 million people.
facts: It was pushed up by the Indian Plate colliding with the Eurasian Plate, and it still grows a few millimeters every year.
Its highest peak, Mount Everest, was remeasured in 2020 and announced at 8,848.86 meters.

nature-009.summary: Arcing across the heart of Europe, the range that feeds great rivers like the Rhine, Rhône and Po, and the stage for the golden age of mountaineering in the 19th century.
facts: Its highest peak, Mont Blanc, rises over 4,800 meters.
The first Winter Olympics were held in 1924 in Chamonix, at the foot of these mountains.

nature-010.summary: Stretching along the western edge of South America through seven countries, the world's longest continental mountain range and the highest outside Asia.
facts: The Inca built Machu Picchu on a ridge here, 2,400 meters above sea level.
Potatoes were first cultivated here before spreading to dinner tables around the world.

nature-011.summary: Running north–south through western North America from Canada to New Mexico, the range along which the continental divide splits waters between the Pacific and the Atlantic.
facts: Denver sits at its foot at 1,600 meters above sea level, earning it the nickname “the Mile High City.”
Yellowstone National Park and Banff National Park both lie within this range.

nature-013.summary: Rising over the Bay of Naples, the volcano that buried Roman towns in AD 79 and, with three million people living within reach, is counted among the world's most dangerous.
facts: Excavation of Pompeii, buried in its ash, began in 1748 and continues to this day.
Its most recent eruption was in 1944.

nature-014.summary: Covering northern Africa from the Atlantic to the Red Sea, the world's largest hot desert, separating the Mediterranean coast from tropical Africa to the south.
facts: Covering about 9.2 million square kilometers, it is larger than the contiguous United States.
It was once a land of grasslands and lakes.

nature-015.summary: Spanning southern Mongolia and northern China, the world's sixth-largest desert, a cold one whose Mongolian name means "waterless land".
facts: In 1923, an American expedition found a trove of fossilized dinosaur eggs here.
The yellow dust that blankets the Korean Peninsula in spring blows in from here and the surrounding deserts.

nature-016.summary: The driest non-polar desert, on Chile's northern Pacific coast, so rich in copper and nitrate that three nations went to war over it in the 19th century.
facts: Some weather stations here have gone decades without a single drop of rain.
Its clear skies have drawn major observatories such as the ALMA radio telescope.

nature-017.summary: In southern Siberia, the world's oldest and deepest lake, over 25 million years old, holding a fifth of the planet's surface fresh water and listed as a World Heritage Site.
facts: The Baikal seal, one of the few freshwater seals, lives nowhere else in the world.
In winter, it freezes so thick that cars drive across it.

nature-018.summary: On the U.S.–Canada border where Lake Erie's water plunges toward Lake Ontario, a major source of hydroelectric power and North America's signature tourist attraction.
facts: In 1901, a woman became the first person to go over it in a barrel and survive.
The largest, Horseshoe Falls, is on the Canadian side, and boats take visitors right up into its spray.

nature-019.summary: Australia's longest river, running from the southeastern highlands to the Southern Ocean and forming the border between New South Wales and Victoria.
facts: The Murray–Darling Basin is Australia's most important region for irrigated farming.
So much water is drawn off that sand has been dredged from its mouth since 2002 to keep it from closing up.

nature-020.summary: Running north–south through western Russia from the Arctic coast to the Kazakh steppe, the ancient range conventionally taken as the boundary between Europe and Asia.
facts: Rich deposits of iron and copper gave rise to industrial cities such as Yekaterinburg.
Though not very high, it stretches 2,500 kilometers from north to south.

nature-021.summary: On the Zambezi River at the Zambia–Zimbabwe border, the world's largest single sheet of falling water and a World Heritage Site.
facts: Its local name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, means “the smoke that thunders.”
In 1855, David Livingstone became the first European to see it and named it after the British queen.

nature-022.summary: On the East African plateau, the lake from which the White Nile flows, Africa's largest by area and the world's largest tropical lake.
facts: About half of its area belongs to Tanzania, 45 percent to Uganda and 6 percent to Kenya.
Nile perch introduced in the 1950s pushed out many native fish species.

nature-023.summary: A red-sand semi-desert in the interior of southern Africa, where the Okavango's marshes in the northwest teem with wildlife.
facts: It covers most of Botswana, and the San people have lived here for 20,000 years.
After rain, grass briefly springs up and turns it into something like a grassland.

nature-024.summary: Africa's second-longest river, crossing the rainforests of Central Africa to the Atlantic, with the world's second-largest drainage basin after the Amazon.
facts: Some stretches are more than 220 meters deep, making it the deepest river in the world.
Two capital cities, Kinshasa and Brazzaville, face each other across it.

nature-025.summary: Rising across the Maghreb of North Africa, the range that separates the Sahara from the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts and has long been home to the Berbers.
facts: It runs about 2,500 kilometers across Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, and its highest peak, Toubkal, reaches 4,167 meters.
Legend says the Titan Atlas, who held up the sky in Greek mythology, was turned to stone and became these mountains.

nature-026.summary: A coastal desert stretching over 2,000 kilometers along the Atlantic from Angola to South Africa, considered the oldest desert in the world.
facts: At Sossusvlei, red sand dunes over 300 meters tall stand in rows.
It is home to a beetle that drinks by catching the morning fog on its back.

nature-027.summary: Lying at the bottom of a rift valley between Jordan, Israel and the West Bank, a salt lake whose shores are the lowest land on Earth and whose brine keeps bathers afloat.
facts: Its surface lies about 440 meters below sea level.
Because the rivers feeding it are diverted for use, its level drops about 1 meter every year.

nature-028.summary: Lying between Europe and Asia and fed 80% by the Volga, the world's largest lake by area and a center of the oil industry.
facts: It is about 1.7 times the size of the Korean Peninsula and is bordered by five countries, including Russia and Iran.
Caviar, made from sturgeon eggs, comes from here.

nature-029.summary: Flowing from the Tibetan Plateau through six Southeast Asian countries to the South China Sea, the region's lifeline, whose basin is second only to the Amazon in biodiversity.
facts: In Vietnam, where its mouth splits into many branches, it is called the Cửu Long, meaning “Nine Dragons.”
More than half of Vietnam's rice comes from the delta at its mouth.

nature-030.summary: Winding across northern China to the Bohai Sea laden with loess, the cradle of ancient Chinese civilization, known as China's "mother river".
facts: Its course has shifted dramatically many times throughout history.
Its frequent floods earned it the name “China's Sorrow.”

nature-031.summary: The world's second-highest peak, in the Karakoram on the Pakistan–China border, long so deadly that about one climber died for every four who reached the top.
facts: Its name was given in 1856 by a British survey team as shorthand for the second peak in the Karakoram.
The first winter ascent was not achieved until 2021.

nature-032.summary: The highest peak of the Alps on the France–Italy border, whose first ascent in 1786 is traditionally seen as the start of modern mountaineering.
facts: Its name means “White Mountain,” and the logo of the pen maker that shares its name depicts its snowcapped summit.
In 1965, an 11.6-kilometer tunnel bored beneath it connected the two countries.

nature-033.summary: Flowing from the Swiss Alps through Germany and the Netherlands to the North Sea, once a frontier of the Roman Empire and now a backbone of Europe's inland shipping.
facts: Its castle-lined middle gorge became a World Heritage Site in 2002.
The Lorelei, the rocky cliff made famous by Heine's poem, stands on its banks.

nature-034.summary: Rising on the east coast of Sicily, Italy's tallest peak south of the Alps and one of the most active volcanoes in the world.
facts: Records of its eruptions go back more than 3,000 years.
The volcanic soil on its slopes nurtures grapes and citrus.

nature-035.summary: Europe's longest river, flowing through the heart of western Russia into the Caspian Sea, regarded as Russia's national river and affectionately called "Mother".
facts: The folk song “Song of the Volga Boatmen” was sung by the laborers who hauled boats upstream.
The Battle of Stalingrad was fought on its banks.

nature-036.summary: A warm sea bounded by Central America, the north coast of South America and the West Indies, home to about 9% of the world's coral reefs.
facts: It was a stage for pirates in the 17th and 18th centuries, and the film “Pirates of the Caribbean” takes its title from it.
Its name comes from the Carib people, who lived in the region when Christopher Columbus arrived.

nature-037.summary: Running from the Rocky Mountains through the arid American Southwest toward Mexico's Gulf of California, the river that carved the Grand Canyon.
facts: So much of its water is drawn off that since the 1960s it has rarely reached the sea.
Forty million people in seven states rely on it for water and electricity.

nature-038.summary: The largest and highest of the Great Lakes, straddling the U.S.–Canada border, and the world's largest freshwater lake by area.
facts: About two-thirds of its area lies in the United States, with the rest in Canada.
In 1975, the freighter Edmund Fitzgerald sank in it during a storm.

nature-039.summary: North America's highest peak, the centerpiece of a national park in the Alaska Range, and the world's northernmost mountain over 6,000 meters.
facts: Its Native name, Denali, was restored in 2015, but in 2025 the U.S. government changed it back to McKinley.
Its rise from base to summit is greater than that of Mount Everest.

nature-040.summary: Mexico's second-highest peak, in the central volcanic belt, an active volcano that reawakened in 1991 and looms over the capital, Mexico City.
facts: Its name means “smoking mountain” in Nahuatl.
Major eruptions sometimes force nearby airports to close.

nature-041.summary: Where a tributary of the Paraná plunges over a 2.7-kilometer cliff in the rainforest, the world's largest waterfall system, a World Heritage Site in two countries' national parks.
facts: They straddle the border between Brazil and Argentina.
The deepest part is called the “Devil's Throat.”

nature-042.summary: Covering the great river basin of northern South America, more than half of the planet's remaining tropical forest and the most species-rich place on Earth.
facts: One in ten known species lives here.
About 60% of the forest lies within Brazil.

nature-043.summary: On the high Andean plateau, South America's largest lake by both volume and area, a mythical place and pilgrimage site for the Incas.
facts: Peru and Bolivia share the lake between them.
People live on islands woven from reeds.

nature-044.summary: Flowing some 4,880 kilometers from southern Brazil to Argentina, a major South American waterway linking inland cities to the sea.
facts: The Itaipu Dam, built jointly by Brazil and Paraguay, harnesses the river, and the two countries share its power.
It joins the Uruguay River to form the Río de la Plata estuary.

nature-045.summary: Arcing across the floor of the western Pacific near Guam, the deepest trough on Earth, formed where the Pacific Plate dives beneath another plate.
facts: Even Mount Everest turned upside down would leave over 2,000 meters to spare.
The bathyscaphe Trieste reached the bottom in 1960, and James Cameron did so in 2012.

nature-046.summary: Running parallel to Australia's east coast and sending rivers either to the coast or inland, the longest mountain chain lying entirely within a single country.
facts: Even its highest peak, Mount Kosciuszko, is a modest 2,228 meters.
The Blue Mountains near Sydney are part of the chain.

nature-047.summary: Lying just south of the equator north of Australia, an island holding the world's third-largest rainforest and the richest plant diversity of any island.
facts: More than 800 languages are spoken here.
Though it lies near the equator, a few glaciers survive on its high mountains, but they are on the verge of disappearing.

nature-048.summary: An island state across the sea south of mainland Australia, where about a fifth of the land is protected as World Heritage and the world's first green party was born.
facts: The Tasmanian devil, a pouched carnivore, lives in the wild almost only on this island.
About 11,700 years ago, rising seas created the Bass Strait and separated it from the mainland.

nature-049.summary: New Zealand's highest peak, rising in the Southern Alps that run down the South Island, officially renamed in 1998 with its Māori name placed first.
facts: A 1991 rockslide knocked 10 meters off its summit.
Before conquering Mount Everest, Hillary climbed its south ridge in 1948.

nature-050.summary: Spanning Western Australia and South Australia, the continent's largest desert, where most inhabitants are Indigenous peoples such as the Pitjantjatjara.
facts: In the 1950s, the United Kingdom carried out nuclear tests at Maralinga in this desert.
Explorer Ernest Giles, who first crossed it in 1875, named it after Queen Victoria.
